content: The University of Hong Kong, commonly abbreviated as HKU and pronounced as Hong Kong U, is the oldest tertiary institution in Hong Kong. Its motto, Sapientia et Virtus, translates to wisdom and virtue. English is the official language of instruction at the university. Reputation In 2006, HKU was ranked 33rd globally and 3rd among universities in Greater China by the Times Higher Education Supplement. It was also included in Newsweek's 2006 rankings of the Top 100 Global Universities. History HKU traces its origins to the Hong Kong College of Medicine for Chinese, established in 1887 by the London Missionary Society. The university itself was founded in 1910 under the proposal of Sir Frederick Lugard, then Governor of Hong Kong, who sought to establish a university in China to compete with other Western powers, particularly Prussia, which had recently opened Tongji University in Shanghai. The foundation stone of the Main Building was laid on March 16, 1910. Lugard envisioned the university as a means to educate Chinese students in British imperial values rather than those of other Western powers. The university's establishment was made possible through funding and support from the government and the business sector in southern China, both of which were eager to learn the technological advancements of the West following the Industrial Revolution. HKU initially opened with a Faculty of Medicine, which evolved from the Hong Kong College of Medicine. Within a year, the Faculties of Engineering and Arts were also established. The university held its first congregation in December 1916, graduating 23 students. Initially an all-male institution, it began admitting female students in 1927. In 1937, Queen Mary Hospital was opened and has since served as the university's teaching hospital. Before World War II, HKU had four faculties: Arts, Engineering, Medicine, and Science. The university was temporarily closed during the war but reopened afterward, undergoing significant structural development as part of post-war reconstruction efforts. The Faculty of Social Sciences was established in 1967, followed by the Department of Law in 1969. The Faculty of Dentistry, based at the Prince Philip Dental Hospital, was established in 1982 and remains Hong Kong's only faculty training dental professionals. In 1984, the School of Architecture and the School of Education became full-fledged faculties, and a separate Faculty of Law was created. The Faculty of Business and Economics was established in 2001 as the university's youngest faculty. HKU has nurtured the largest number of research postgraduate students in Hong Kong, comprising approximately 10% of its total student population. All ten faculties and departments provide teaching and supervision for research students (MPhil and PhD), with administration overseen by the Graduate School. About 45% of the university's academic staff are recruited from overseas. In 2001, HKU celebrated its 90th anniversary, publishing Growing with Hong Kong: HKU and its Graduates – The First 90 Years as an impact study on its graduates' contributions to various fields in Hong Kong. In January 2006, the Faculty of Medicine was renamed the Li Ka Shing Faculty of Medicine in recognition of a HK$1 billion donation from Mr. Li Ka Shing and his foundation. Campus and History The main campus of HKU spans 160,000 square meters on Bonham Road and Pok Fu Lam Road in the Mid-levels of Hong Kong Island. Many of its buildings are among the few remaining examples of British Colonial architecture in Hong Kong. The Faculty of Dentistry is located at the Prince Philip Dental Hospital in Sai Ying Pun. The university also operates the Kadoorie Agricultural Research Center in the New Territories and the Swire Institute of Marine Science at the southern tip of the d'Aguilar Peninsula on Hong Kong Island. Main Building The oldest structure at HKU, the Main Building, was constructed between 1910 and 1912 with funding from Sir Hormusjee Naorojee Mody. Designed by architects Messrs Leigh & Orange, it features a post-Renaissance style with red brick and granite. The building's main elevation is marked by four turrets and a central clock tower, a gift from Sir Paul Chater in 1930. Originally used as classrooms and laboratories for the Faculties of Medicine and Engineering, it now houses various departments within the Faculty of Arts. The central Great Hall, named Loke Yew Hall after an early benefactor, was declared a monument in 1984. Hung Hing Ying Building Opened in 1919 and financed by Sir Paul Chater, Professor G.P. Jordan, and others, this Edwardian-style building originally housed the student union. It was later used for administrative purposes and is now home to the Department of Music. The building was declared a monument in 1995. Tang Chi Ngong Building Constructed in 1929 with a donation from Mr. Tang Chi-ngong, this building was originally intended for the teaching of Chinese language and literature. It now houses the Centre of Asian Studies and was declared a monument in 1995. University Museum and Art Gallery The Fung Ping Shan Museum, built in 1932 as a library for Chinese books, was converted into a museum for Chinese art and archaeology in 1962. It houses collections of ceramics, pottery, and bronzes. In 1996, the T.T. Tsui Building was added to form the University Museum and Art Gallery. Administration The Chancellor of HKU is the Chief Executive of Hong Kong, currently the Honorable Donald Tsang. The Pro-Chancellor is the Honorable Dr. David Li, and the Vice-Chancellor is Professor Lap-Chee Tsui. The university employs over 800 academic staff. Research and Endowment HKU is a founding member of Universitas 21, an international consortium of research-led universities. It benefits from substantial government funding, although recent salary reductions have impacted this advantage. Thirty-nine academic staff members are ranked among the world's top 1% of scientists by the ISI based on citation records. Demographics In 2005-2006, HKU had a student population of 21,508, including 11,584 undergraduates, 7,928 taught postgraduates, and 1,996 MPhil/PhD students. The university attracts some of the best students in Hong Kong, admitting around 50% of all Grade-A students from the Hong Kong A-level examinations. Academic Units HKU comprises ten faculties: Architecture, Arts, Business and Economics, Dentistry, Education, Engineering, Law, Medicine, Science, and Social Sciences. It also operates the School of Professional and Continuing Education (SPACE), which offers a range of programs, including language courses and sub-degree programs. Student Services HKU provides various services to meet students' personal needs, including career education, counseling, health services, and recreational facilities. Student Life HKU encourages hall education, where students learn through participation in hall-based activities. However, recent scandals involving bullying and inappropriate orientation activities have raised concerns about hall culture. Criticisms HKU has faced criticism for its bias toward medical disciplines, with humanities and social sciences suffering from chronic underfunding. The university has also faced challenges to academic freedom, most notably in 2000 when allegations of political interference in research led to a public controversy. Future Development HKU plans to build a new Centennial Campus west of the Main Campus, with construction beginning in 2008 and completion expected by 2011. The university aims to enhance academic research and promote continuing education through improved links with SPACE.
